expectedText:
VOCATIONAL TRAINING COUNSELOR EVALUATIONS IN SPOUSAL SUPPORT PROCEEDINGS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · John Doe

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Vocational Training Counselor Evaluations in Spousal Support Proceedings Information Sheet concerns Jane Doe and John Doe, who were married on June 1, 2010 and separated on January 1, 2026, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation filed or to be filed in the California superior court for Los Angeles County. It describes a specific chapter of California's Family Code governing spousal support upon dissolution or legal separation (Family Code Chapter 3, Sections 4330 through 4339): the court's general authority to set a support amount and duration, the self-sufficiency advisement a court may give a supported party, the court's authority to order an examination by a vocational training counselor and that counselor's required qualifications, mandatory findings on the marital standard of living, retroactivity of a support order, termination of a contingent support order and the resulting refund obligation, termination of support on death or remarriage, and the order in which property is resorted to when enforcing a spousal support order. It is not itself a request for order, notice of motion, declaration, or court order, and completing it does not create, modify, terminate, or enforce any spousal support obligation between Jane Doe and John Doe. Only a court order, applying these statutes to the facts of an actual pending or completed proceeding, can do that.

COURT'S AUTHORITY TO ORDER SPOUSAL SUPPORT BASED ON THE MARITAL STANDARD OF LIVING
In a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation, California's Family Code authorizes a court to order one party to pay the other party support in an amount, and for a period of time, that the court determines is just and reasonable. The statute directs that this determination be based on the standard of living established during the marriage, taking into consideration the circumstances set out in a separate chapter of the Family Code governing spousal support factors. This is the general, post-judgment order-making authority for spousal support; it operates once a judgment of dissolution or legal separation is entered, rather than while the case is only pending.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) In a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties, the court may order a party to pay for the support of the other party an amount, for a period of time, that the court determines is just and reasonable, based on the standard of living established during the marriage, taking into consideration the circumstances as provided in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 4320)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4330(a) (California Legislative Information text), the court's general authority to order post-judgment spousal support based on the marital standard of living (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4330.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (Family Code Section 4330(a)); no additional independent source was found for it. By its own terms, this subsection's grant of authority is tied to "a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties" — it does not on its face extend to a judgment of nullity, unlike the temporary (pendente lite) support authority addressed elsewhere in this corpus, which by its own text does reach nullity proceedings. This clause does not restate or quote the multi-factor list in the chapter it cross-references ("Chapter 2, commencing with Section 4320"); that separate chapter's factors are addressed in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document. The statute does not itself define "just and reasonable" or set any numeric cap on amount or duration.

COURT'S DISCRETION TO ADVISE A SUPPORTED PARTY OF AN EXPECTATION OF SELF-SUPPORT
When making a spousal support order, California's Family Code permits, but does not require, a court to advise the party receiving support that the recipient should make reasonable efforts to assist in providing for their own support needs. The statute directs that any such advisement take into account the same particular circumstances the court considered under the spousal-support-factors chapter it cross-references. The statute separately allows a court to decide the advisement is inadvisable in the case of a marriage of long duration, a term the Family Code defines and addresses in a different, adjoining section of this same chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) When making an order for spousal support, the court may advise the recipient of support that the recipient should make reasonable efforts to assist in providing for their support needs, taking into account the particular circumstances considered by the court pursuant to Section 4320, unless, in the case of a marriage of long duration as provided for in Section 4336, the court decides this warning is inadvisable."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4330(b) (California Legislative Information text), the court's discretionary authority to advise a supported party of an expectation of self-sufficiency (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4330.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (Family Code Section 4330(b)); no additional independent source was found for it. The statute uses the word "may" for the advisement itself and for a court's decision that the advisement is inadvisable in a long-duration marriage — both are discretionary, not mandatory, on the face of this text. This clause does not quote Family Code Section 4336, which the subsection cross-references for the definition and consequences of a "marriage of long duration"; that section already has a verified, quoted clause elsewhere in this corpus. The statutory text itself does not use the term "Gavron warning" — that is a term of judicial usage from case law, and no case law was independently fetched or verified for this document (see the Deliverables report for the CourtListener rate-limit that prevented case-law research in this session). The statute does not specify any required form, wording, or timing for the advisement.

COURT'S AUTHORITY TO ORDER A VOCATIONAL TRAINING COUNSELOR EXAMINATION
In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation, California's Family Code authorizes a court to order a party to submit to an examination by a vocational training counselor. The examination must include an assessment of that party's ability to obtain employment, based on the party's age, health, education, marketable skills, employment history, and the current availability of employment opportunities, with the examination's focus on whether the party could obtain employment that would allow the party to maintain the marital standard of living. The statute limits when such an order may be made: only on motion, for good cause, and on notice to the party to be examined and to all parties, with the order itself required to specify the time, place, manner, conditions, and scope of the examination and who is to conduct it. A party who does not comply with such an order is subject to the same consequences that apply to noncompliance with an examination ordered under a specified chapter of the Code of Civil Procedure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court may order a party to submit to an examination by a vocational training counselor. The examination shall include an assessment of the party’s ability to obtain employment based upon the party’s age, health, education, marketable skills, employment history, and the current availability of employment opportunities. The focus of the examination shall be on an assessment of the party’s ability to obtain employment that would allow the party to maintain their marital standard of living.(b) The order may be made only on motion, for good cause, and on notice to the party to be examined and to all parties. The order shall specify the time, place, manner, conditions, scope of the examination, and the person or persons by whom it is to be made.(c) A party who does not comply with an order under this section is subject to the same consequences provided for failure to comply with an examination ordered pursuant to Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 2032.010) of Title 4 of Part 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4331(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), the court's authority to order a vocational training counselor examination, the procedural prerequisites for the order, and the consequence of noncompliance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4331.)
  Known gap: Family Code Section 4331(a), (b), and (c) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text, not because they are independent sources stitched together — no ellipsis or omitted text separates them. This clause does not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced Code of Civil Procedure provision, Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 2032.010) of Title 4 of Part 4, which defines the actual consequences for noncompliance; it states only that Section 4331(c) points to that chapter. The statute does not itself say who bears the cost of the examination — that is addressed by a separate subsection, Section 4331(f), covered in a different clause in this document, and the two are not combined here because a quote spanning (c) through (f) would also have to reproduce (d) and (e), the counselor-qualification provisions.

REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS OF A VOCATIONAL TRAINING COUNSELOR AND ALLOCATION OF COST
California's Family Code defines a "vocational training counselor," for purposes of an examination ordered in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding, as an individual with sufficient knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education in interviewing, administering and interpreting marketable-skills tests, formulating career goals, planning courses of training and study, and assessing the job market, so as to qualify as an expert in vocational training under a specified section of the Evidence Code. The statute lists minimum qualifications such a counselor must have: a master's degree in the behavioral sciences or another postgraduate degree the court finds sufficient; qualification to administer and interpret career-potential inventories; demonstrated ability in interviewing clients and assessing marketable skills, with an understanding of age, health, education, experience, and mobility constraints; knowledge of current employment conditions, job markets, and wages in the relevant geographic area; and knowledge of local education and training programs, with their costs and time plans. Separately, the statute authorizes a court to order the supporting spouse to pay the necessary expenses and costs of counseling, retraining, or education, in addition to spousal support.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) “Vocational training counselor” for the purpose of this section means an individual with sufficient knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education in interviewing, administering, and interpreting tests for analysis of marketable skills, formulating career goals, planning courses of training and study, and assessing the job market, to qualify as an expert in vocational training under Section 720 of the Evidence Code.(e) A vocational training counselor shall have at least the following qualifications:(1) A master’s degree in the behavioral sciences, or other postgraduate degree that the court finds provides sufficient training to perform a vocational evaluation.(2) Qualification to administer and interpret inventories for assessing career potential.(3) Demonstrated ability in interviewing clients and assessing marketable skills with an understanding of age constraints, physical and mental health, previous education and experience, and time and geographic mobility constraints.(4) Knowledge of current employment conditions, job market, and wages in the indicated geographic area.(5) Knowledge of education and training programs in the area with costs and time plans for these programs.(f) The court may order the supporting spouse to pay, in addition to spousal support, the necessary expenses and costs of the counseling, retraining, or education."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4331(d)-(f) (California Legislative Information text), the definition and minimum qualifications of a vocational training counselor, and the court's authority to allocate the cost of counseling, retraining, or education (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4331.)
  Known gap: Family Code Section 4331(d), (e), and (f) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text; this is one statutory section, not three independent sources. This clause does not independently fetch or verify Evidence Code Section 720, which subsection (d) cross-references for the general expert-witness-qualification standard. The statute does not itself define how much postgraduate training a court must find "sufficient" under subsection (e)(1) for a non-master's-degree counselor to qualify — that determination is left to the court. The cost-allocation authority in subsection (f) is worded as "may order," so it is discretionary rather than mandatory, and it applies only to "the supporting spouse" paying costs — the statute's text examined here does not describe any mechanism for a supported spouse to be ordered to pay these costs.

MANDATORY FACTUAL FINDINGS ON THE MARITAL STANDARD OF LIVING
In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation, California's Family Code requires the court to make specific factual findings on the standard of living established during the marriage. The statute separately requires the court, at the request of either party, to make appropriate factual determinations with respect to other circumstances. The standard-of-living finding this statute requires is what the general spousal-support order-making authority elsewhere in this same chapter directs the court to base its support amount and duration on.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall make specific factual findings with respect to the standard of living during the marriage, and, at the request of either party, the court shall make appropriate factual determinations with respect to other circumstances."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4332 (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory factual findings on the marital standard of living (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4332.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code Section 4332); no additional independent source was found for it. The statute does not specify a required format, level of detail, or timing for these "specific factual findings," and it does not itself define what "other circumstances" a party may request findings on beyond the standard-of-living finding — it states only that the court "shall make appropriate factual determinations" on request.

RETROACTIVITY OF A SPOUSAL SUPPORT ORDER
California's Family Code permits a spousal support order made in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation to be made retroactive. The retroactivity the statute describes runs to the date of filing the notice of motion or order to show cause that requested the support order, or to any subsequent date the court chooses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An order for spousal support in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties may be made retroactive to the date of filing the notice of motion or order to show cause, or to any subsequent date."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4333 (California Legislative Information text), the court's authority to make a spousal support order retroactive to the filing of the request or a later date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4333.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code Section 4333); no additional independent source was found for it. On its face, the statute permits retroactivity only back to the filing date of the request for the order (or a later date) — it does not authorize retroactivity to a date before that filing, such as the date of separation or the date of marriage. The statute's use of "may be made retroactive" is permissive, not mandatory, and it does not list any factors a court must weigh in deciding whether, or to what date, to make an order retroactive.

TERMINATION OF CONTINGENT SPOUSAL SUPPORT AND THE RESULTING REFUND OBLIGATION
Where a court orders spousal support for a contingent period of time, California's Family Code provides that the supporting party's obligation terminates when the contingency happens, and the court may order the supported party to notify the supporting party, or that party's attorney of record, when the contingency occurs. If the supported party fails to give that notice and continues to accept spousal support payments, the statute requires the supported party to refund the payments that accrued after the contingency happened, with any overpayment applied first to spousal support payments then in default.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) If a court orders spousal support for a contingent period of time, the obligation of the supporting party terminates on the happening of the contingency. The court may, in the order, order the supported party to notify the supporting party, or the supporting party’s attorney of record, of the happening of the contingency.(b) If the supported party fails to notify the supporting party, or the attorney of record of the supporting party, of the happening of the contingency and continues to accept spousal support payments, the supported party shall refund payments received that accrued after the happening of the contingency, except that the overpayments shall first be applied to spousal support payments that are then in default."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4334(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), termination of a contingent spousal support order and the refund obligation for payments accepted after the contingency occurred (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4334.)
  Known gap: Family Code Section 4334(a) and (b) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text; this is one statutory section, not two independent sources. This statute governs only a support order for "a contingent period of time" — it is distinct from, and this document does not address, either the non-extension rule for a support order with a fixed, non-contingent end date under a separate section of this same chapter (Section 4335), or the automatic termination of support on death or remarriage addressed in a different clause in this document (Section 4337). The statute does not itself define what qualifies as a "contingency" for this purpose, and the notification requirement ("the court may, in the order, order the supported party to notify") is discretionary, contingent on the court including it in the order, rather than an automatic statutory duty.

AUTOMATIC TERMINATION OF SPOUSAL SUPPORT ON DEATH OR REMARRIAGE
California's Family Code provides that a party's obligation under a spousal support order terminates automatically upon the death of either party, or upon the remarriage of the party receiving support. This default rule applies except to the extent the parties have agreed otherwise in writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as otherwise agreed by the parties in writing, the obligation of a party under an order for the support of the other party terminates upon the death of either party or the remarriage of the other party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4337 (California Legislative Information text), the automatic termination of a spousal support obligation on death or remarriage, absent a contrary written agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4337.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code Section 4337); no additional independent source was found for it. The statute is a default rule only: it expressly yields to a written agreement of the parties providing otherwise, so it does not, by itself, determine the outcome in every case. This document does not address the separate question of a written agreement's own requirements or effect, which is addressed elsewhere in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement and Premarital Agreement documents. The statute uses "remarriage" without further definition, and does not address the effect of a registered domestic partnership on the termination rule.

ORDER IN WHICH PROPERTY IS RESORTED TO WHEN ENFORCING A SPOUSAL SUPPORT ORDER
When enforcing an order for spousal support, California's Family Code directs the court to resort to specified categories of property in a set order. First is the earnings, income, or accumulations of either spouse after the date of separation that would have been community property had the spouses not separated. Next is the community property, then the quasi-community property, and finally the other separate property of the party required to make the support payments.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In the enforcement of an order for spousal support, the court shall resort to the property described below in the order indicated:(a) The earnings, income, or accumulations of either spouse after the date of separation, as defined in Section 70, which would have been community property if the spouse had not been separated from the other spouse.(b) The community property.(c) The quasi-community property.(d) The other separate property of the party required to make the support payments."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 4338 (California Legislative Information text), the required order of resort to a party's property when enforcing a spousal support order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=4338.)
  Known gap: Family Code Section 4338's introductory clause and subsections (a) through (d) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text; this is one statutory section. This clause does not independently fetch or quote Family Code Section 70, which subsection (a) cross-references for the definition of "date of separation" — that definition is addressed elsewhere in this corpus (the Postnuptial Agreement document). This statute governs only the order of resort to property in enforcing an already-existing spousal support order; it does not by its own text govern the initial characterization or division of community, quasi-community, or separate property in the underlying dissolution or legal separation.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature of Jane Doe: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual request for order, notice of motion, or other pleading concerning spousal support, filed with the California superior court for Los Angeles County. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that filing, and it does not create, modify, terminate, or enforce any spousal support obligation between Jane Doe and John Doe; only a court order, applying Family Code Sections 4330 through 4339 and the related sections they cross-reference to the facts of an actual proceeding, does that.]

The retroactivity the statute describes runs to the date of filing the notice of motion or order to show cause that requested the support order, or to any subsequent date the court chooses.

expectedJSON.body: Where a court orders spousal support for a contingent period of time, California's Family Code provides that the supporting party's obligation terminates when the contingency happens, and the court may order the supported party to notify the supporting party, or that party's attorney of record, when the contingency occurs. If the supported party fails to give that notice and continues to accept spousal support payments, the statute requires the supported party to refund the payments that accrued after the contingency happened, with any overpayment applied first to spousal support payments then in default.

citations.cite: termination of a contingent spousal support order and the refund obligation for payments accepted after the contingency occurred
citations.quote: (a) If a court orders spousal support for a contingent period of time, the obligation of the supporting party terminates on the happening of the contingency. The court may, in the order, order the supported party to notify the supporting party, or the supporting party’s attorney of record, of the happening of the contingency.(b) If the supported party fails to notify the supporting party, or the attorney of record of the supporting party, of the happening of the contingency and continues to accept spousal support payments, the supported party shall refund payments received that accrued after the happening of the contingency, except that the overpayments shall first be applied to spousal support payments that are then in default.

This default rule applies except to the extent the parties have agreed otherwise in writing.

Next is the community property, then the quasi-community property, and finally the other separate property of the party required to make the support payments.
